messages.subject: vastly different density estimates from secr and oSCR
messages.subject_clean: vastly different density estimates from secr and oSCR
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am helping someone analyze camera trap data with a multi-session SCR model. Initially, I used oSCR for the analysis but I have now re-analyzed the data with secr and am getting density estimates an order of magnitude lower.
I am taking into account the different spatial resolutions of the two packages and fitting structurally the same model to the same data. It's a 'vanilla' model: Euclidean distance, no telemetry data, Poisson observation model...
I have more experience with secr than oSCR (the secr estimates are also much more in line with previous analyses of subsets of the same data), so am assuming I am doing something wrong in the oSCR analysis. But I have been scouring the data and code and cannot find my mistake.
I have attached an Rmarkdown report showing data comparison and model fitting for the two packages. This is only for a single-session subset of the data, to speed up computations, but the problem persists when analyzing all sessions. The data aren't mine to share publicly, but I would be happy to share the data subset and script used for the report off-list if it helps figuring out what is going wrong.
Thanks in advance!
Best,
Rahel

Hi Andy,
it's one of those study areas where the trap array really spans the entirety of the population (a national park) and the buffer is habitat that animals use to some degree (so you can't really remove it from S) but you'd expect a much lower density. But if you calculate abundance for the area of the trap array based on the two density estimates, the secr one is quite low (apprx 1200km2 *0.3/100km for 3.6 animals) whereas the oSCR one is absurdly high (9/100km2 for >100 animals).
And you're right, even though the detection parameters look good, the sex ratio is off as well.
Best
Rahel

messages.body_plain:
this is interesting.   I guess what the oSCR model is thinking is that the Pr(capture a male) is about 1.0, whereas Pr(capture a female) is very low, so the population has a whole bunch of uncaptured Females out there but not many uncaptured males. That makes sense just looking at the data.  But the SECR results are somewhat consistent in telling the same story, just less extreme.

There's one way to get to the bottom of this, but I don't see how to do this easily:  you need to compute the likelihood either using the oSCR or SECR likelihood for both sets of parameters and see which one is best.  I think it could be done by hacking the oSCR.fit function (you use the MLE as starting values and just return the evaluation of the likelihood).  Not sure about SECR....

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andy,
I agree about the sparse data but - in the full analysis we have 4 years of data and we're not estimating session specific sex ratios or detection parameters, and still, the estimates from oSCR are 10x higher than those from secr.
Cheers
Rahel

On Fri, Apr 5, 2024 at 3:10 PM Jeffrey Royle <jar...@gmail.com> wrote:

> just fyi I think the likelihood is very flat in the psi.sex dimension and the algorithm is stopping too soon (one or the other) or else there's multi-modes to the likelihood which would NOT be surprising given the sparsity of F captures and the fact that you have 3 parameters to describe the F data!
>
> On Fri, Apr 5, 2024 at 9:05 AM Jeffrey Royle <jar...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > this is interesting.   I guess what the oSCR model is thinking is that the Pr(capture a male) is about 1.0, whereas Pr(capture a female) is very low, so the population has a whole bunch of uncaptured Females out there but not many uncaptured males. That makes sense just looking at the data.  But the SECR results are somewhat consistent in telling the same story, just less extreme.
> >
> > There's one way to get to the bottom of this, but I don't see how to do this easily:  you need to compute the likelihood either using the oSCR or SECR likelihood for both sets of parameters and see which one is best.  I think it could be done by hacking the oSCR.fit function (you use the MLE as starting values and just return the evaluation of the likelihood).  Not sure about SECR....
> >
> >
> >
> > On Fri, Apr 5, 2024 at 8:53 AM Rahel Sollmann <rasr...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > >

Hi Andy,
so I think I calculated the log-LL values under secr and oSCR for estimates from both model versions (no guarantee that I got the oSCR hacking right, it is Friday afternoon...):
The nice thing is, secr outputs the LL values as it runs the model so that one was easy.
secr LL:
         (1) for estimates from secr: -258.723
         (2) for estimates from oSCR: -29489.761
oSCR LL (assuming oSCR spits out the negLogLik, I multiplied the output by -1):
         (1) for estimates from secr: -1951.324
         (2) for estimates from oSCR: -1710.763
So... very weird, no?
Any other thoughts?
Thanks and happy weekend,
Rahel

messages.subject_clean: Can the effects be linear?
messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

I feel like there is an easy answer to this, that ranges from either simply transform your variable or its just the way the scr models work..but I will ask it anyways because its something I’ve often struggled with.

In most cases I expect linear relationships between the covariates of interest and density. There are cases where an optimum might be expected (hump shape) or perhaps a non-linear in some cases. But the simplest spot to start is one unit of resource equals one unit of animal density. However, due to the nature of the scr models (poisson and binomial forms) the relationship between the covariates and density can become non linear, even though the underlying model is a linear model. For hypothesis testing this might not matter much. But for predicting density across large areas, and especially extrapolation, these non-linear results with density create some headaches and problematic predictions near the tails. The non-linear relationships are also not necessarily biologically defensible.

What are the approaches to try and “straighten” out these lines? Some are straight, but it depends on the magnitude of the effect, and whether it pushes the result near 0 within the range of the covariate.

Best regards,
Clayton

Good idea on quadratics. I’ve got those running now.

Realism—I think the non-linear results that emerge between covariates and density are unrealistic at times. Here’s an example, it’s not egregious, but works. % canopy cover on the x, grizzly density on y. In the simplest case I’d expect as there are more trees, there is less sun hitting the ground, and eventually less food for bears. As a first guess I’d expect this to be linear. Density declines by about the same amount between 0-10% canopy as it does between 10-60% canopy.

Extrapolation issues are their own issue, I agree. When you extrapolate outside your covariate space it is well known to create issues. My point was that these non-linear results can make that issue even worse. If I had data on bear density from 7-60% canopy I’d feel like I had decent coverage of the space. But when I extrapolate even a little below 7% I get huge increases in density due to that non-linear effect.

I think there are a few things going on.  One is that you have to be careful with interpreting marginal effects plots, especially in your situation where you have a good number of covariates with explanatory power.  I have to assume that some of the covariates are correlated, even to a small degree (r > 0.3)  This can make the isolated effect of canopy cover hard to interpret at certain ends of the spectrum, where the multi-dimensional attributes never exist in the exact combination illustrated (e.g., 10% canopy cover at average values of all other covariates, assuming you standardized).

Also, I'd still argue that 0% canopy cover is a condition that you did not sample, and thus any extrapolation below 7% could be unreliable.

You have some nice examples of covariates with effect sizes that are relatively small (human density) versus large (canopy cover), and then relationships that are linear (black bear) versus non-linear (human density).  Transforming your covariate might help if you think the nature of the relationship is not being properly accommodated. Otherwise, it's hard to see a problem with what you've got here.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Chris,

Thank you so much for your reply. I appreciate your help! I apologise for the late feedback - did not notice your email previously and when I did so it was already almost one year late and at that time I was on the genetics part which took me some time.

To refresh, we modelled  the spatiotemporal hedgehog density with an 11-year search-based SCR dataset, with habitat composition and distance to the nearest badger setts (d2badger) included as density covariates. As one new badger sett was identified halfway, we got two different d2badger surfaces. We modelled the effects by taking the two d2badger surfaces in the ssDF file in one SCR framework - for years before the new badger sett one d2badger file was listed into, and for years after another. The results showed the negative effects of d2badger, and also in this way, we got two sets of estimated hedgehog density surfaces - one before and another after the new badger sett. I think the method is fine? May I have your opinion on this please? Previously I tried to include session*d2badger but got high standard errors which might be due to our limited dataset.

Another question is about how to deal with the input dataset. Our yearly search effort was quite varied (9 - 81 search nights per year with ~500 nights in total). Originally, when each search night was treated as an occasion, the software did not run with like "out of boundaries" returned. So we shrank the max no. occasion to 80, and then each time by 5 until it was 60,  it started to run smoothly. So, our method was like this: each search night was defined as an occasion with the exception for years 2010,  2012, 2013,  2021, in which the numbers of search nights were larger than 60 (62, 81, 67, 64, respectively), and were shrank to 60 occasions with two nights as an occasion for a small number of occasions, to make the software to run because the software was failed to perform with our dataset when with 81, 80, 75, 70, or 65 occasions was included in a session. (I did this following Dr Andrew Royle's suggestion on a similar issue in a group discussion.) So, now when the max no. occasion was set to 60, the captures that occurred in extra nights were considered (although a small number and the majority were recaptures on that occasion and finally not taken into account in the modelling). Another possible way to limit the max no. occasion to 60 is by cutting off the extra nights and all captures occurred in those nights. Both methods did not affect the final results in a considerable way based on many tests, but I still wish to know: which process to deal with the input data is more reasonable - to keep the extra captures or totally remove? I prefer the former for more captures (although a little bit) for better modelling the habitat effects as our data size is limited for running complex models (some generated high SEs). If to remove all extra captures, the search effort is to be better accounted for (although still a little bit) by keeping each search night as an occasion which should be more desirable for year-specific densities (although the effect is negligible as tested). The year-specific densities (with D~ Session, each year as a session) were with high SEs for all single sessions (close or even higher than the estimates) and either to keep to removing the extra captures did not improve this. (As tested at least 3 years of data combined as one session is needed for an accurate session-specific density, if with SE < 20% estimate as a threshold).

Thank you for reading my long email. I hope I have made it clear. But if any more information is needed, please let me know. Thank you in advance!

Best regards,

Hongli

Hongli Yu
PhD student
ARES, Nottingham Trent University
